strengths: The authors propose a novel application of oblique decision trees in the online group fairness setting.

The work is original as it explores the novel application of oblique decision trees in the context of group-fair online predictions; the authors provide key insights and explore the novel adaptation of oblique decision trees for efficient training and introduce theoretical lemmas to show the relationship of the complexity, fairness performance and the modeling choices, e.g., the depth of the tree.

The authors have presented a work of good quality; the paper provides extensive theoretical complexity analyses and evaluations for demographic parity fairness on multiple modalities of data (tabular, image, and language), and includes extensive ablation studies to empirically show the properties and behavior of the proposed method.

The authors do a good job in making the paper clear to read; the scenario is clearly defined, the intuitions clearly stated, and the modeling is explained in clear language and terms, making the article relatively easy to follow even without understanding of oblique decision trees.

In my opinion, the work can be significant in showing how to adapt a powerful tree-based model for online predictions with fairness as an important consideration, especially for tabular data where tree-based models have been shown to perform better; the proposed model may prove to be a useful tool in the practitioner’s toolbox for online predictive systems where fairness is also important.
The paper is well written, the problem is well motivated, and results are promising.

An interesting aspect of the proposed approach is that the group fairness objective (DP) is imposed at a local level (in each node), which may reduce disparities in DP across different regions of the input space, and the method has online characteristics (no need to store previous data, no need to query the model multiple times).
The theoretical analysis provided is reasonable, motivating and providing some grounded guarantees on the proposed solution.
The proposed Aranyani framework has the potential to be a groundbreaking adjustment in online learning algorithms, paving the way for enhanced fairness in this domain.

The research stands out due to its unique experimental environment settings and innovative adjustments in the problem formulation, presenting a fresh perspective by introducing a new idea in online learning.

While there are certain ambiguities concerning the linkage between foundational knowledge and experimental configurations, the paper's narrative is cohesively structured and of commendable quality; the meticulous mathematical proofs for each Aranyani property add depth and credibility.

Aranyani's design, which negates the need to store individual data instances, is especially significant for data privacy, addressing storage challenges and emphasizing operation based on aggregate statistics rather than individual data points.
This paper proposed an effective approach called Aranyani and provides solid theoretical analysis for it.
This study focuses on a unique and critical problem wherein machine learning fairness is examined in an online context, with individual sample instances observed sequentially.

The paper introduces an effective framework for forward and backward propagations that leverages statistical summaries from previous samples to address computational complexities associated with retaining all prior samples.
The presented algorithm consistently surpasses baseline techniques across all tasks and is both empirically and theoretically robust and comprehensive.
weaknesses: The evaluations only show demographic parity results; the authors provide no results for other group-fairness notions based on the true label (e.g., equalized odds or equal opportunity), making it unclear if the method can effectively balance accuracy and fairness when the fairness metric is conditioned on the true label.

The results do not have error bars, making it difficult to compare methods without considering variance across different initializations; the absence of mean and variance reporting hampers assessment of robustness and reliability given the stochastic nature of the optimization process.

It is unclear what the fairness dynamic looks like for different methods across time as training proceeds; the lack of temporal analysis of how the fairness measure varies across time steps limits understanding of the method's behavior in a dynamic environment.

Appendix results show that fairness result variance increases significantly when moving from a single tree to a forest, contradicting the expectation that ensemble methods reduce variance; this aspect is not well discussed and the reason for variance increase with more trees is unclear.

Figure 4 (right) includes error bars, but it is not clear how the variance is measured (whether across time steps) and why tree depth impacts the variance of fairness so greatly; the lack of clarity on the source of variance makes interpretation difficult.
Fairness performance degrades considerably when the tree depth is higher, which may limit the expressivity of the model; the trade‑off between fairness and expressivity needs further exploration.

There are no ablation studies showing the impact of the particular loss used to measure fairness (e.g., Huber loss versus ℓ₂ loss or hinge loss); the choice of loss function is critical and its sensitivity remains unanswered.
An empirical runtime analysis comparing the proposed method to other methods is missing; understanding practical runtime performance is crucial for real‑world applications.
Figure 4 (right) does not have any legend, making it difficult to understand which line/symbol corresponds to which metric.
The Aranyani triangle symbol in the text does not match the plots.

It is unclear how to guarantee that each leaf contains samples from both sensitive groups; if not guaranteed, the handling of nodes with samples from a single sensitive group and the scalability to multiple groups are not addressed.

A discussion on the δ and λ parameters from Eq.4 is missing; λ should be set based on ε (DP constraint) from Eq 2, and the Huber loss not being zero when the ε constraint is satisfied raises questions about the approach to enforce the fairness constraint.
The algorithm or a simplified pseudocode of the proposed framework should be provided to aid understanding and reproducibility.

The manuscript would benefit from a more detailed breakdown of the concluding stages of the training process; it is uncertain whether the oblique decision tree is designed as an end‑to‑end neural network or follows the training pattern of standard tree models with a neural configuration.
Deeper insights are needed regarding Aranyani's subdued performance on the COMPAS dataset; there may be challenges using Aranyani for datasets with fewer than 7k entries.
While the paper indicates that Aranyani is more suited to trees of limited height, alternative approaches for cases requiring greater tree height should be explored.
Observing Aranyani's functionality in intricate real‑world situations beyond benchmark datasets would add depth to the findings.
Including more recent fairness representation learning models (modified for online environments) as baselines would be valuable for comparative analysis.
Legends are necessary in Figure 4 (right) to distinguish which line represents accuracy.
The main use cases for achieving fairness in this online setting are missing, making the motivation of the work lack justification.

The problem setting should be stated more clearly; the paper seems to assume that previous data points are not available, which is unclear compared to typical online learning that processes one data point at a time but also has feedback from previous data points.
Authors do not clearly state the goal in the online setting; it is unclear what the right fairness metric for online settings is and whether fairness is measured for the entire dataset at each step.

Using the aggregate of past statistics to adjust model parameters poses a challenge because model parameters shift with each time step, potentially causing past statistics to diverge from what would be obtained using all previously stored data; the conditions under which aggregated past gradients work need elaboration.

If the model consistently underperforms, it could cause a shift in data distribution, e.g., the minority group might stop supplying data for updates; the authors should discuss how the proposed algorithm would operate under such circumstances.
